claims.text: High-entropy alloys can be used to produce a ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
High-entropy alloys have inherent resistance to temper embrittlement.
Resistance to temper embrittlement enables the proposed ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
The proposed starting material is an FCC high-entropy alloy.
The proposed starting material is in the annealed state.
The intervention consists of isothermal holding at 500°C for 100 hours.
The isothermal treatment is conducted under vacuum and stress-free conditions.
The treatment produces grain-boundary segregation of solute atoms.
Suppression of grain-boundary embrittlement improves ductility.
Isothermal holding increases Charpy impact toughness by 20% relative to the as-cast state.
Temper-embrittlement resistance may depend on the specific high-entropy-alloy composition and processing conditions.

contradictions.description: The intervention is specified for an annealed FCC alloy, but the predicted outcome and falsification comparison use an as-cast baseline. Thus, heat-treatment effects are confounded with the difference between annealed and as-cast initial states.

The hypothesis proposes a ductile–brittle–ductile transition, but the predicted outcome specifies only a net toughness increase and does not define or predict the intervening brittle state required for such a transition.
